title: The Shema and the Trinity

keyTerms.d: Israel’s central confession, prayed twice a day by the observant Jew: “Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). It is the first prayer a Jewish child learns and traditionally the last words of the dying; the closest thing Judaism has to a creed. Its theme is unmistakable — there is one God, and Israel belongs to him alone.

The Hebrew word translated “one” in the Shema. Is saying: the ordinary Hebrew cardinal number, which in context can describe a unity made of parts (“one flesh”), because the plurality is supplied by the noun it modifies, not by the number. Not saying: it does NOT by itself prove plurality in God or the Trinity — the “compound unity” argument is a discredited overreach, and the echad-versus-yachid contrast cannot bear the doctrinal weight some place on it. The case for the triune God rests on divine identity and 1 Corinthians 8:6, never on this one word.

Richard Bauckham’s phrase for how ancient Jews defined God — less by abstract metaphysics than by identity: who God is and what only God does (God alone is sole Creator of all things, God alone is sovereign Ruler of all things). To include Jesus in that identity is not to make him a second god but to confess that the one God of Israel is somehow Father and Son together. The framework is widely influential, though the divine-identity category is itself debated: Larry Hurtado reframes the same data as a pattern of devotion, and James F. McGrath disputes the category.

Writing to Corinth around AD 53–54 against idolatry, Paul takes the creed’s two titles for the one God — theos (“God”) and Kyrios (“Lord”) — and distributes them: “one God, the Father… and one Lord, Jesus Christ.” He has not added a second deity alongside the Shema; he has reached inside it and placed Jesus within it. This reading (Bauckham, N. T. Wright) is influential, arguably dominant among New Testament scholars, but genuinely contested, not unanimous — James F. McGrath reads “one Lord” as set alongside the creed, not inside it.

In the Greek Shema Paul knew (the Septuagint), Kyrios is not a generic word for a master; it is the standard reverent rendering of the unspeakable divine name YHWH. That is why Paul’s pairing of the creed’s “one God” with “one Lord, Jesus Christ” is so weighty — he gives Jesus the creed’s own divine title.

The Jewish and Unitarian reading, drawn from the Hebrew Bible and Second Temple Judaism: an exalted intermediary — personified Wisdom, the great angels, exalted patriarchs like Enoch — can bear God’s name and do God’s work without being God, and the risen Jesus is slotted into that role of supreme agent. The motif is genuinely present, but it breaks at one point: cultic worship.

The Shema’s exclusivity is stated outright elsewhere in the recurring declaration that there is no god besides YHWH — the “there is no other” (’ên ’ôd) formula of Deuteronomy 4:35, 39; 1 Kings 8:60; and Isaiah 45:5–6, 21–22 (with the parallel “there is no god beside me” of Deuteronomy 32:39) — which Bauckham treats as a defining mark of ancient Jewish monotheism.

What Jewish monotheism guarded jealously for God was not the posture of homage — Israelites could bow before a king as well as before the LORD (1 Chronicles 29:20) — but the substance of worship: sacrifice, invocation, prayer. The angels of Second Temple Judaism refuse worship and redirect it to God (Revelation 19:10); yet the earliest Christians prayed to Jesus, were baptized in his name, sang to him, and called on him — a devotional pattern Judaism reserved for God alone (Hurtado).

derive.q: The popular move says “one flesh,” “one cluster” prove echad means a compound unity — so the Shema itself hints at plurality in God. Does the word echad carry that?
derive.ans: no — the plurality is in the noun, not the number
derive.why: The plurality in “one flesh” (Genesis 2:24) or “one cluster” (Numbers 13:23) does not come from echad at all; it comes from the noun it modifies. Echad is the ordinary Hebrew cardinal “one” — it routinely describes things that are emphatically singular. So on this lexical point the critics are right, intellectual honesty requires saying so plainly, and the echad-versus-yachid contrast cannot bear the weight some place on it.

derive.q: Paul knew the Shema in Greek: theos and Kyrios, two titles both naming the one God. In 1 Corinthians 8:6 he assigns theos to the Father and Kyrios to Jesus. So he has placed Jesus…?
derive.ans: inside the creed, not beside it
derive.why: Paul takes the creed’s two words for the one God and distributes them — “one God, the Father… and one Lord, Jesus Christ.” He has not added a second deity alongside the Shema; he has reached inside it and placed Jesus within it. On the reading we defend — arguably dominant, though genuinely contested — this is christological monotheism: the one divine identity, confessed under both of the creed’s titles.

derive.q: He does this in a chapter attacking idolatry, over against “many ‘gods’ and many ‘lords.’” If “one Lord” were a second, lesser deity, Paul would be…?
derive.ans: committing in verse 6 the idolatry he condemns in verse 5
derive.why: This is not a Gentile convert centuries later but a trained Pharisee within roughly two decades of the crucifixion, handling the most protected sentence in his religion. If Paul thought he were smuggling a second, lesser divine being into the picture, he would be committing in verse 6 precisely the sin he condemns in verse 5. The natural reading is that he saw no contradiction at all.

derive.q: Kyrios in the creed is the Septuagint’s rendering of the divine name. So if “one Lord” is a being who is NOT the one God, you do not get strict monotheism — you get…?
derive.ans: a second power, not unitarian monotheism
derive.why: Kyrios is not a generic word for a master; in the Shema it is the rendering of the divine name itself. So if “one Lord” means a being who is not the one God — a separate, exalted creature through whom all things were made — Paul has confessed one God plus one additional divine-but-not-God Lord. That is not the strict monotheism the objection wants to protect; it is a second power. The reading that actually preserves monotheism is the trinitarian one.

derive.q: Exalted agents — Wisdom, the great angels, Enoch — could be entrusted with God’s name and his works. What one thing did none of them ever receive?
derive.ans: the cultic worship reserved for God alone
derive.why: Grant that God’s name and functions could be entrusted to a supreme agent — the worship itself still could not be. The angels of Second Temple Judaism refuse worship and redirect it to God; no intermediary figure that we know of was ever placed inside the Shema — Philo’s “second god,” the Logos, is the nearest case, and even it is never placed inside the confession. Wisdom is praised, Enoch is exalted — but Paul put Jesus inside the creed of divine uniqueness, and the earliest churches prayed to him, sang to him, and were baptized in his name.

derive.q: Grant the whole reading. Does 1 Corinthians 8:6, by itself, prove the Trinity?
derive.ans: no — it clears the charge; the positive case rests on revelation and the resurrection
derive.why: It does not. It does not show the Trinity is taught in Deuteronomy 6:4, and grammar alone was never going to decide the question. What the argument establishes is that the Shema does not foreclose the question of the one God’s inner life, and that the earliest Christians recited it with Jesus inside — monotheism kept, not monotheism lost. This clears the charge against the Trinity; the positive case rests on revelation and on the historical case for who Jesus was.

honestState.p1: The lexical leg is the one to give away, and honesty requires saying so plainly: echad is the ordinary Hebrew numeral, the echad-versus-yachid contrast cannot bear the doctrinal weight some place on it, and the popular “compound unity” argument is a discredited overreach the case does not use. The weight does not sit on the lexicon at all; it sits on 1 Corinthians 8:6 — a trained Pharisee distributing the creed’s own two titles between Father and Son, within two decades of the crucifixion, in a chapter against idolatry. That reading is influential, arguably dominant among New Testament scholars, but genuinely contested, not unanimous.
honestState.fairness: The strongest scholarly critic is James F. McGrath, who argues directly against Bauckham and Wright that “one Lord” is set alongside the Shema, not folded into it; a wider literature debates whether “splitting,” “supplementing,” or “brokering” best describes what Paul does, and the Bauckham–Wright reading — supported by Hurtado and, more cautiously, by James D. G. Dunn — is not the settled view. Two further honesties are owed. The traditional Jewish reading of the Shema is a serious and ancient interpretation, held in good faith by people who love this text; the Christian claim is not that Jews have failed at arithmetic but an intra-biblical claim they are entitled to find unpersuasive. And Daniel Boyarin’s thesis that “binitarian” ideas once circulated within Judaism is suggestive, not decisive — and must be kept sharply distinct from the stronger Barker–Lang claim that ancient Israel actually worshipped two gods, which Bauckham judges the evidence does not support, the surviving literature of Second Temple Judaism being uniformly monotheistic.
honestState.verdict: The honest answer to the question is no: the Shema does not rule out the Trinity, and the objection built on it does not hold. But be exact about what the argument does. It has not shown that the Trinity is taught in Deuteronomy 6:4; it has not shown that echad “means” a compound unity; and it has not refuted the traditional Jewish reading by force of grammar alone. What it establishes is that the Shema confesses one God and does not, by itself, foreclose the question of that God’s inner life — and that the earliest Christians, Jewish monotheists led here by a Pharisee writing against idolatry, did not abandon the Shema when they confessed Jesus as Lord; they recited it, with Jesus inside it: monotheism kept, not monotheism lost. This argument does not prove the Trinity; it clears the charge against it. The positive case rests on revelation and on the historical case for who Jesus was — and this is what we hold to be true: the one God exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, three coequal, coeternal persons, one God.

order: The Shema asserts YHWH’s exclusive, unique deity over against the gods of the nations; it does not address how many persons that one God is — and the popular “echad means compound unity” argument does not work and is not used here.
In 1 Corinthians 8:6 Paul — a trained Pharisee — restates the Shema with Jesus inside it, distributing the creed’s own titles (theos, kyrios) between Father and Son.

Therefore the Shema does not rule out the Trinity: on the reading we defend (arguably dominant, though contested), the earliest Christology placed Jesus inside the unique divine identity of Israel’s God — monotheism kept, not abandoned.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its precision check.
cards.a: The Shema asserts YHWH’s exclusive, unique deity over against the gods of the nations; it does not address how many persons that one God is. Precision: no one should claim the Trinity is “stated” in Deuteronomy 6:4 — that reads the New Testament back into a text written centuries before it. And the popular “echad means compound unity” argument does not work and is not used here.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and its precision check.
cards.a: In 1 Corinthians 8:6 Paul distributes the creed’s own two titles, theos and kyrios, between Father and Son: “one God, the Father… and one Lord, Jesus Christ.” Precision: he has not added a second deity alongside the Shema; he has reached inside it. This reading is influential, arguably dominant, but genuinely contested — it does not show the Trinity is taught in Deuteronomy 6:4.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the Shema does not rule out the Trinity, and the objection built on it does not hold: the earliest Christians recited the creed with Jesus inside it — monotheism kept. It does not, by itself, prove the Trinity, settle the question by grammar, or refute the traditional Jewish reading; it clears the charge. The positive case rests on revelation and the resurrection.

cards.q: Why is the echad “compound unity” argument NOT run here?
cards.a: Because honesty requires saying so plainly: echad is the ordinary Hebrew numeral, the plurality in “one flesh” belongs to the noun, and the echad-versus-yachid contrast cannot carry the weight some place on it. Only the negative survives — the creed is aimed at rival gods, not at a person-count, so it does not forbid internal complexity. The weight sits on 1 Corinthians 8:6, not on the lexicon.

cards.q: What does Paul do with the creed’s two titles in 1 Corinthians 8:6?
cards.a: In the Greek Shema both theos (God) and kyrios (Lord) name the one YHWH. Paul takes those two words for the one God and distributes them — theos to the Father, kyrios to Jesus — inside a sentence that still confesses one. He reaches into the creed and places Jesus within the identity of the one Lord of Israel.

cards.q: Why can “one Lord” not simply mean a lesser being?
cards.a: Because in the Shema Paul quotes, kyrios IS the divine name, the LXX rendering of YHWH, and the chapter opposes “many gods and many lords.” A separate, created creator-lord would be one God plus one divine-but-not-God Lord — a second power — which is the very idolatry Paul is refuting. The coherent reading is one divine identity, two persons sharing the creed’s two titles.

cards.q: Reply to: “through whom” makes Jesus a mere instrument lower than the Father.
cards.a: Creating is the act that marks the absolute line between God and everything else: “I am the LORD, who made all things… who alone stretched out the heavens” (Isaiah 44:24). The one through whom all things were made cannot be among the things that were made. And the prepositions do not mark rank — Romans 11:36 piles “from him and through him and to him” onto God without distinction.

cards.q: Where did Jewish monotheism draw the line — and how is Jesus treated at it?
cards.a: Not at the posture of homage (Israelites could bow before a king as well as the LORD, 1 Chronicles 29:20) but at the substance of worship — sacrifice, invocation, prayer. The angels of Second Temple Judaism refuse worship and redirect it to God; yet the earliest Christians prayed to Jesus, sang to him, and were baptized in his name.

cards.q: What two things distinguish Jesus from every exalted intermediary figure?
cards.a: First, the boundary of worship: Wisdom, the angels and Enoch receive no cultic devotion and redirect worship to God, while the earliest Christians offered Jesus the devotion Judaism reserved for God alone. Second, no intermediary figure we know of was ever placed inside the Shema (Philo’s Logos is the nearest case, and even it is never placed inside the confession). Wisdom is praised; Enoch is exalted; but Paul put Jesus into the creed of divine uniqueness itself.

cards.q: Reply to: this is one verse from one unusually creative theologian.
cards.a: 1 Corinthians 8:6 reads less like a doctrine Paul invented than a confession he quotes — compact, balanced, assumed as common ground. And it does not stand alone: the Philippians 2 hymn, widely regarded as pre-Pauline, gives Jesus Isaiah 45’s every-knee oath; the Aramaic churches cried Marana tha to Jesus before Greek theology existed; baptism ran in the threefold name (Matthew 28:19). Paul is the earliest window onto this devotion, not its inventor.

cards.q: What is the honest scope — what does this argument NOT do?
cards.a: It does not prove the Trinity is in Deuteronomy 6:4, it does not make echad “mean” a compound unity, and it does not refute the traditional Jewish reading by grammar alone — a reading held in good faith, which grammar was never going to decide. It clears the charge against the Trinity; the positive case rests on revelation and on who Jesus was shown to be.

cards.q: Does this reading make Jesus a second god — or collapse the Father into the Son?
cards.a: Neither. It confesses one God, not two (that would be the polytheism Paul is condemning), and it keeps the persons distinct: Father and Son share the one undivided divine identity under the creed’s two titles — the Father is not the Son. The Trinity is a doctrine of monotheism: one God, rich enough to be Father, Son, and Spirit.

obj.q: Echad just means “one.” The “compound unity” move — one flesh, one cluster — is apologetic spin, reading the Trinity into a number.
obj.model: Agreed — and we do not run that argument. Echad is the ordinary numeral, the plurality in “one flesh” belongs to the noun, and the echad-versus-yachid contrast cannot carry the weight some place on it. What survives is only the negative: the creed is aimed at rival gods, not at a person-count, so it does not forbid internal complexity. The Shema leaves the door ajar; 1 Corinthians 8:6 is what walks through it, and that is where the whole weight of this argument sits.

obj.q: Paul confesses the one God of the Shema, the Father, and sets “one Lord, Jesus Christ” alongside that confession, not inside it. Jesus is the exalted Messiah, God’s supreme agent bearing God’s name — as Second Temple Judaism exalted Wisdom, the great angels and Enoch without making them God (James F. McGrath).
obj.model: Then which “Lord”? In the Shema Paul quotes, kyrios IS the divine name — the LXX rendering of YHWH. On that reading Paul confesses one God plus one additional non-God creator-Lord — inside an anti-idolatry argument. That is not unitarianism; it is a second god. The coherent reading: one divine identity, two persons sharing the creed’s two titles. And if an agent could bear God’s name, grant it: the name could be entrusted to a supreme agent, but the worship could not.

obj.q: Second-Temple Judaism exalted intermediary figures — personified Wisdom, the great angels, exalted patriarchs like Enoch — who do God’s work and even bear God’s name without being God. Slotting the risen Jesus into that role of supreme agent is striking, but it is not the Nicene Trinity.
obj.model: The agency literature is real — and its boundary is what Jesus crosses: those figures refuse worship (Revelation’s angel: “worship God!”), receive no cultic devotion, and are never put inside the Shema. Homage alone was not the line (Israel bowed to God and king, 1 Chronicles 29:20); what Judaism guarded for God alone was the substance of worship: sacrifice, invocation, prayer. Prayers to Jesus, baptism in his name, YHWH-texts transferred to him — Hurtado documents a worship-pattern Judaism reserved for God alone.

obj.q: Two millennia of Jewish scholarship read the Shema as excluding all of this. The custodians of the creed outrank one Pharisee.
obj.model: Paul WAS a custodian — “as to the law, a Pharisee” — as were the “great many of the priests” (Acts 6:7) and the believing Pharisees (Acts 15:5) in the earliest church; this is an intra-Jewish reading. The exclusion hardened in later polemic — understandable history, not neutral arbitration. And the older strata complicate the confidence: Word, Wisdom and Spirit acting as God, the two-powers debates the rabbis fought over Daniel 7’s “one like a son of man,” who comes with the clouds — a suggestive, contested line of evidence (Boyarin), not a proof. The argument asks the creed’s question with the creed’s own materials. Grammar alone was never going to decide it; the case rests on what the one God has since disclosed in Christ.

unseen.q: Even granting all of it — 1 Corinthians 8:6 names one God and one Lord. That is two, not three. Where is the Spirit? At best you have a binity, not the Trinity.
unseen.model: That is a fair and exact reading of the verse, and the argument does not pretend otherwise: 1 Corinthians 8:6 is not offered as a proof-text for the whole Trinity. What it shows is the hard part — that the earliest Christians placed Jesus inside the Shema, within the unique identity of the one God, rather than beside it as a second deity. That this argument does not, by itself, prove the triune God is not a dodge; it is the honest scope. It clears the charge that confessing Jesus as Lord breaks the creed; it does not, on its own, establish the full doctrine. And the verse does not stand alone. The same confession of divine oneness is already shared out across Father, Son, and Spirit in independent streams older than any Greek theology: the threefold name into which the church baptized (Matthew 28:19), and the liturgical cadence of “one body… one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Ephesians 4:4–6). So the Spirit is not an afterthought bolted on at Nicaea; the raw material the creeds later organized is already in the earliest practice. This argument does not prove the Trinity; the positive case rests on revelation and on the historical case for who Jesus was. But this is what we hold to be true, and the one verse is one true strand of it: the one God exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — three coequal, coeternal persons, one God.
